newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Monitors see Pakistan vote defects, but minor ones.
newsitem.headline: Monitors see Pakistan vote defects, but minor ones.

text.p: The leader of a Commonwealth team of observers said it had found shortcomings in Monday's national and provincial elections in Pakistan but not of the scale that could have changed the outcome.

In an interim statement to a news conference a few hours after the polling, former Australian prime minister Sir Malcolm Fraser said a low turnout of voters was a "serious message" from them to political parties after the dismissal of three elected governments in eight years.
"It is clear that public respect for political parties has plummeted and democratic government discredited," he said.

But Fraser said his team was satisfied all those who wished to vote were able to do so, political parties were free to campaign and for the first time universal adult franchise was extended to tribal areas bordering Afghanistan.

"There were shortcomings," he said, adding that his team's observers noted that some polling stations did not open on time and the legal necessity for a voter to possess a national identity card was "clearly open to abuse".
"It is alleged that names appeared on the roll of more than one polling station. Women in parts of the country are still discouraged from exercising their right to vote," he said.
"However, none of these shortcomings was, in our judgement, of a scale or character as to have been likely to produce a different outcome."
Fraser said his team's observers had asked the party workers at different polling booths if they were happy with the arrangements and "overwhelmingly the answer to that was 'yes'".
Fraser spoke before any results had been announced in the election, which Benazir Bhutto's main rival, former prime minister Nawaz Sharif, was widely expected to win.
